newsitem.title: LATVIA: JELGAVA IN SMALL Q1 PROFIT, SEES '97 BREAKEVEN.
newsitem.headline: JELGAVA IN SMALL Q1 PROFIT, SEES '97 BREAKEVEN.

text.p: Latvia's Jelgava construction material factory said on Tuesday that it made a symbolic profit during the first quarter of 1997 against losses of 27,000 lats and was expecting to get close to breakeven this year.
"We broke even during the first quarter as we registered a symbolic profit of 112 lats," Andris Pavitols, the manager of the Jelgava company told Reuters.
"We plan to break even this year and increase the production volume of our main product by 15 percent," Pavitols said.
He said the firm produced some 3,000 tonnes of its main product last year and had some 50,000 lats worth of produce sitting in stock.
The company had losses of 105,000 lats on turnover of 75,000 lats in 1995.

"We are now producing European quality wall and ceiling constructions which are three times cheaper than in the EU but the crux of the problem is the lack of purchasing power in Baltics," Pavitols said.
"I would expect a take-off in sales in two years perhaps," he added.
"Our products are traditionally bought by the middle class, compared for example to Lode Brick now being bought by those more affluent," Pavitols said.
The company began exporting woodwool building materials to the other two Baltic countries last year, with 25 percent of the total production sold to Estonia and Lithuania.
Separate sales to Kaliningrad, Poland and Denmark were quite rare but Jelgava plans more sales on these markets this year.
Jelgava is currently utilising only 7.5 percent of its capacity, close to 40,000 cubic metres of wall and ceiling constructions a year.
The company this year has restarted wood processing by producing window-frames, doors and floor boards.
"Although the machines we use are comparatively old, we look forward to earning some 20,000 lats to 40,000 lats this year on wood-processing," Pavitols said.
The company is currenlty in talks with the local council over the capitalisation of some 80,000 lats of debts.
"This would leave some six percent of our share capital in the municipality's hands," Pavitols said.
